preamble: In Aramaic, Proto-Semitic *ṣ́, reconstructed as an ejective lateral fricative [ɬʼ], ends up as the voiced pharyngeal fricative [ʕ], merging with ʿayin, where Hebrew and Akkadian have ṣ and Arabic ḍ: Syriac ʾarʿā 'earth' against Hebrew ʾéreṣ and Arabic ʔarḍ. Older texts (Old Aramaic, some Imperial and Biblical Aramaic) write the sound with qoph: Imperial Aramaic 𐡀𐡓𐡒 and Biblical Aramaic ארק 'earth', Old Aramaic 𐤌𐤓𐤒 'illness', beside Imperial Aramaic 𐡌𐡓𐡏 already with ʿayin and Syriac məraʕ; Wikipedia's correspondence table gives the Aramaic reflex as *ṣ́, written q, later ʿ. Which sound the q spelling stood for is not settled by these sources. Aramaic treats the other emphatic fricative *ṯ̣ differently, merging it with ṭ. The Proto-Semitic value is a reconstruction: whether the emphatics were ejective or pharyngealized is debated, since the daughter languages differ (pharyngealized in Arabic, Aramaic and Tiberian Hebrew, glottalized in Ethiopian Semitic and Modern South Arabian), though they are generally reconstructed as glottalized, i.e. ejective (Cantineau 1952; Kogan 2011: 61, as cited by Wikipedia; Wikipedia, Proto-Semitic language), and the most accepted view makes only *ṣ an affricate [tsʼ], leaving *ṣ́ a fricative [ɬʼ] (Kogan 2011: 62, cited by Wikipedia), while 'maximal' accounts reconstruct the affricate [tɬʼ]; the Greek rendering Mátlia of Geʽez ḍ has been taken as evidence for an affricate in Geʽez (Rodinson 1981 and Weninger 1998, per Kogan 2011: 80, cited by Wikipedia). This entry follows the [ɬʼ] of Wikipedia's Proto-Semitic consonant table.

examples.to: Imperial Aramaic 𐡀𐡓𐡒, Biblical Aramaic ארק; later Jewish Babylonian Aramaic אַרְעָא ʾarʿā, Syriac ܐܰܪܥܳܐ ʾarʿā
examples.note: Written with q first, with ʿ later (Wiktionary). Compare Hebrew ʾéreṣ, Arabic ʔarḍ.

examples.to: Old Aramaic 𐤌𐤓𐤒 'illness', Imperial Aramaic 𐡌𐡓𐡏 'illness', Syriac ܡܪܥ məraʕ 'to be ill, sick'
Jewish Aramaic עָנָא ʿānā, Syriac ܥܳܢܳܐ ʿānā
Aramaic אָעָא ʾāʿā, עָעָא ʿāʿā, עָקָא ʿāqā
examples.note: The variant ʿāqā keeps the q spelling.

examples.to: Syriac ʕrṭ '(pa.) to break wind', ʕurṭē 'flatulence'

sources: Kogan, L. (2011). Proto-Semitic Phonetics and Phonology. In S. Weninger (Ed.), The Semitic Languages: An International Handbook, 54–151. De Gruyter.
